claim: In rat axons, mitochondria respond to glucose levels by halting active transport in high glucose regions.
source: In rat axons, mitochondria respond to glucose levels by halting active transport in high glucose regions.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established observation.

claim: Physiological brain glucose levels fall within the limited range necessary for metabolic enhancement through mitochondrial localization.
source: Our estimates indicate that physiological brain glucose levels fall within the limited range necessary for metabolic enhancement.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling work presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mitochondrial localization is a plausible regulatory mechanism for neuronal metabolic flexibility in the presence of spatially heterogeneous glucose.
source: Hence mitochondrial localization is shown to be a plausible regulatory mechanism for neuronal metabolic flexibility in the presence of spatially heterogeneous glucose, as may occur in long processes of projection neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cells can substantially enhance their metabolism by localizing specific enzymes in regions of high metabolic demand.
source: By localizing specific enzymes in regions of high metabolic demand (Laughton et al., 2007; Zecchin et al., 2015), as well as clustering together consecutively acting enzymes (O'Connell et al., 2012), cells have the potential to substantially enhance their metabolism.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Mammalian neuron axons can grow to lengths on the meter scale.
source: Spatial organization is particularly critical in highly extended cells, such as mammalian neurons, whose axons can grow to lengths on the meter scale.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about neuronal anatomy.

claim: Metabolic demand in neurons is spatially and temporally heterogeneous.
source: Metabolic demand in neurons is spatially and temporally heterogeneous, with especially rapid ATP turnover found in the presynaptic boutons (Rangaraju et al., 2014), and ATP requirements peaking during synaptic activity and neuronal firing (Shulman et al., 2004; Ferreira et al., 2011; Weisová et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Neurons rely primarily on glucose as the energy source for meeting metabolic demands.
source: Neurons rely primarily on glucose as the energy source for meeting these metabolic demands (Peppiatt and Attwell, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Glucose supply can vary substantially over different regions of the neuron due to long lengths of neural processes.
source: Due to the long lengths of neural processes, the glucose supply can vary substantially over different regions of the cell (Ferreira et al., 2011; Weisová et al., 2009; Hall et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: In myelinated neurons, glucose transport into the cell is localized primarily to narrow regions around the nodes of Ranvier.
source: In myelinated neurons, for instance, it has been speculated that glucose transport into the cell is localized primarily to narrow regions around the nodes of Ranvier (Magnani et al., 1996; Harris and Attwell, 2012; Rosenbluth, 2009), which can be spaced hundreds of microns apart (Ibrahim et al., 1995; Butt et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations and is described as speculative.

claim: Glucose transporters in neurons dynamically mobilize to active synapses, providing a source of intracellular glucose heterogeneity.
source: Glucose transporters in neurons have also been shown to dynamically mobilize to active synapses, providing a source of intracellular glucose heterogeneity (Ashrafi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Varying levels of activity in the mammalian brain may lead to varying extracellular glucose levels, resulting in spatially heterogeneous nutrient access.
source: Furthermore, varying levels of activity in the mammalian brain may lead to varying extracellular glucose levels, resulting in spatially heterogeneous nutrient access (Hawkins et al., 1979).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and uses the word 'may', indicating some speculation.

claim: Individual axons have been shown to span across multiple regions of the brain.
source: Individual axons have been shown to span across multiple regions of the brain (Matsuda et al., 2009), enabling them to encounter regions with different glucose concentrations.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Most ATP production in neurons occurs within mitochondria.
source: Most ATP production in neurons occurs within mitochondria: motile organelles that range from interconnected networks to individual globular structures that extend throughout the cell.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about neuronal metabolism.

claim: Mitochondria are critical for neuronal health as energy powerhouses and metabolic signaling centers of the cell.
source: As energy powerhouses and metabolic signaling centers of the cell, mitochondria are critical for neuronal health (Nunnari and Suomalainen, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The spatial organization of mitochondria within the neuron plays a pivotal role in growth and cell physiology.
source: Their spatial organization within the neuron plays a pivotal role in growth and cell physiology (Li et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Defects in mitochondrial transport are involved in the pathologies of several neurological disorders such as peripheral neuropathy and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease.
source: Defects in mitochondrial transport are involved in the pathologies of several neurological disorders such as peripheral neuropathy and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (Baloh, 2008; Baloh et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Mitochondria are localized preferentially to regions of high metabolic demand, such as the synaptic terminals.
source: A number of studies have shown that mitochondria are localized preferentially to regions of high metabolic demand, such as the synaptic terminals (Li et al., 2004; Chang and Reynolds, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Increased Ca2+ levels at active synapses lead to loading of calcium binding sites on Miro, releasing mitochondria from the microtubule and thereby halting transport.
source: Increased Ca2+ levels at active synapses lead to loading of calcium binding sites on Miro, releasing mitochondria from the microtubule and thereby halting transport (Wang and Schwarz, 2009; Macaskill et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: High glucose levels can lead to mitochondrial stalling through the glycosylation of motor adaptor protein Milton by the glucose-activated enzyme O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT).
source: High glucose levels can also lead to stalling, through the glycosylation of motor adaptor protein Milton by the glucose-activated enzyme O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) (Pekkurnaz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The glucose-mediated halting mechanism has been shown to lead to mitochondrial accumulation at glucose-rich regions in cultured neurons.
source: This mechanism has been shown to lead to mitochondrial accumulation at glucose-rich regions in cultured neurons (Pekkurnaz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The glucose-mediated halting mechanism is postulated to regulate mitochondrial spatial distribution, allowing efficient metabolic response to heterogeneous glucose availability.
source: It is postulated to regulate mitochondrial spatial distribution, allowing efficient metabolic response to heterogeneous glucose availability.
evidence: This is described as a postulate, indicating it is a hypothesis or speculation.

claim: Neuronal glucose transporters are bidirectional.
source: Neuronal glucose transporters are known to be bidirectional (Simpson et al., 2007), allowing glucose concentration within the cell to equilibrate with external glucose.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Hexokinase 1 (HK1) is the predominant form of hexokinase expressed in neurons.
source: Hexokinase 1 (HK1), the predominant form of hexokinase expressed in neurons, is known to localize preferentially to mitochondria (John et al., 2011), which in mammalian axons can form individual organelles approximately 1 µm in length (Fawcett, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: HK1 is known to localize preferentially to mitochondria.
source: Hexokinase 1 (HK1), the predominant form of hexokinase expressed in neurons, is known to localize preferentially to mitochondria (John et al., 2011), which in mammalian axons can form individual organelles approximately 1 µm in length (Fawcett, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: In mammalian axons, mitochondria can form individual organelles approximately 1 µm in length.
source: Hexokinase 1 (HK1), the predominant form of hexokinase expressed in neurons, is known to localize preferentially to mitochondria (John et al., 2011), which in mammalian axons can form individual organelles approximately 1 µm in length (Fawcett, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: There is an upper limit on the possible external glucose concentrations that will yield mitochondrial localization at the edges of the domain.
source: There is thus an upper limit on the possible external glucose concentrations that will yield mitochondrial localization at the edges of the domain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: Mitochondria must spend a substantial amount of time in the stationary state for localization to occur, since walking mitochondria will be broadly distributed throughout the domain.
source: Finally, the mitochondria must spend a substantial amount of time in the stationary state, since walking mitochondria will be broadly distributed throughout the domain.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the model.

claim: Very low glucose concentrations will not allow mitochondrial localization because the stopping rate is dependent on glucose concentration.
source: Because the stopping rate is itself dependent on the glucose concentration, this criterion implies that very low concentrations will also not allow mitochondrial localization.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the model.

claim: At high glucose concentrations, approximately 95% of mitochondria are in the stationary state.
source: Experimental measurements indicate that at high glucose concentrations, approximately 95% of mitochondria are in the stationary state (Pekkurnaz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published experimental data.

claim: Physiological brain glucose levels have been measured at 0.7 − 1.3 mM, depending on the brain region.
source: We note that physiological brain glucose levels have been measured at 0.7 − 1.3 mM, depending on the brain region (McNay et al., 2001), implying that glucose-dependent halting of mitochondrial transport would be expected to result in localization of mitochondria at nodes of Ranvier.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published measurements.

claim: Glucose-dependent halting of mitochondrial transport would be expected to result in localization of mitochondria at nodes of Ranvier under physiological conditions.
source: We note that physiological brain glucose levels have been measured at 0.7 − 1.3 mM, depending on the brain region (McNay et al., 2001), implying that glucose-dependent halting of mitochondrial transport would be expected to result in localization of mitochondria at nodes of Ranvier.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing model predictions with physiological measurements.

claim: Localizing mitochondria to the glucose entry points is expected to increase the flux of glucose entering the cell, thereby potentially enhancing the overall metabolic rate.
source: Localizing mitochondria to the glucose entry points is expected to increase the flux of glucose entering the cell, thereby potentially enhancing the overall metabolic rate.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the model.

claim: In hypoglycemic conditions, glucose levels can drop to 0.1 mM.
source: We note that in hypoglycemic conditions, glucose levels can drop to 0.1 mM (Silver and Erecińska, 1994), further increasing the magnitude of this effect.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published measurements.

claim: Intracellular glucose levels could be significantly below the concentrations outside the cell in the case of limited glucose transport into the cell.
source: In the case of limited glucose transport into the cell, intracellular glucose levels could be significantly below the concentrations outside the cell.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the effect of limited transport.

claim: Measurements of intracellular glucose in a variety of cultured mammalian cell types indicate internal concentrations within the range of 0.07 − 1mM, up to an order of magnitude lower than glucose concentrations in the medium.
source: Measurements of intracellular glucose in a variety of cultured mammalian cell types indicate internal concentrations within the range of 0.07 − 1mM, up to an order of magnitude lower than glucose concentrations in the medium (John et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published measurements.

claim: Neuronal cells express a particularly efficient glucose transporter (GLUT3).
source: However, neuronal cells are known to express a particularly efficient glucose transporter (GLUT3) (Simpson et al., 2008), and these transporters have been shown to be highly concentrated near the nodes of Ranvier (Magnani et al., 1996; Rosenbluth, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: GLUT3 transporters have been shown to be highly concentrated near the nodes of Ranvier.
source: However, neuronal cells are known to express a particularly efficient glucose transporter (GLUT3) (Simpson et al., 2008), and these transporters have been shown to be highly concentrated near the nodes of Ranvier (Magnani et al., 1996; Rosenbluth, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Glucose import into the nodes is not rate limiting for myelinated neurons in physiological conditions.
source: We therefore assume that glucose import into the nodes is not rate limiting for myelinated neurons in physiological conditions.
evidence: This is an assumption made in the model based on the properties of GLUT3.

claim: Extracellular brain glucose levels exhibit substantial regional variation, particularly under hypoglycemic conditions where more than ten-fold differences in local glucose concentrations have been reported.
source: Extracellular brain glucose levels exhibit substantial regional variation, particularly under hypoglycemic conditions where more than ten-fold differences in local glucose concentrations have been reported (Paschen et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published measurements.

claim: Individual neurons can traverse multiple different brain regions.
source: Because individual neurons can traverse multiple different brain regions (Matsuda et al., 2009), a single axon can be subjected to heterogeneous glucose levels along its length.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Glucose-dependent mitochondrial localization can play a role in neuronal metabolic flexibility even in the case where glucose entry into the cell is not localized to distinct nodes.
source: This raises the possibility that glucose-dependent mitochondrial localization can play a role in neuronal metabolic flexibility even in the case where glucose entry into the cell is not localized to distinct nodes.
evidence: This is a hypothesis or speculation based on the model.

claim: There is a steep transition between two different regimes when entry and consumption processes are both saturated: one where glucose entry exceeds consumption and internal glucose levels approach external concentrations, and another where consumption dominates and glucose levels drop below saturating concentrations.
source: There is then a steep transition between two different regimes. In one regime, glucose entry exceeds consumption and internal glucose levels approach the external concentrations. In the other, consumption dominates and glucose levels drop below saturating concentrations.
evidence: This is a result from the model analysis.

claim: Neurons are believed to regulate both the density of glucose transporters and hexokinase activity in response to external glucose concentrations and varying metabolic demand.
source: Neurons are believed to regulate both the density of glucose transporters and hexokinase activity in response to external glucose concentrations and varying metabolic demand (Fujii and Beutler, 1985; Robey et al., 1999; Duelli and Kuschinsky, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The physiological range of glucose levels overlaps substantially with the region of high mitochondrial accumulation predicted by the model.
source: We note that the physiological range overlaps substantially with the region of high mitochondrial accumulation, indicating that glucose-dependent halting can modulate mitochondrial distribution under physiologically relevant glycemic levels.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing model predictions with physiological measurements.

claim: By accumulating mitochondria at the cellular region subjected to higher external glucose, the metabolic flux in that region can be substantially enhanced.
source: By accumulating mitochondria at the cellular region subjected to higher external glucose, the metabolic flux in that region can be substantially enhanced.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the model shown in Figure 6e.

claim: The typical physiological range of external glucose levels spans the narrow band of parameter space where metabolic enhancement is expected.
source: It is interesting to note that the typical physiological range of external glucose levels spans the narrow band of parameter space where metabolic enhancement is expected (white lines on Figure 6e,f).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing model predictions with physiological measurements.

claim: Glucose-dependent mitochondrial stopping is a quantitatively plausible mechanism of metabolic flexibility, increasing metabolism in regions with high nutrient availability for axonal projections that span between hypoglycemic and euglycemic regions.
source: These results implicate glucose-dependent mitochondrial stopping as a quantitatively plausible mechanism of metabolic flexibility, increasing metabolism in regions with high nutrient availability for axonal projections that span between hypoglycemic and euglycemic regions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: The magnitude of the metabolic enhancement effect can be tightly controlled by the cell through modulating overall rates of glucose entry and consumption.
source: The magnitude of this effect can be tightly controlled by the cell through modulating overall rates of glucose entry and consumption.
evidence: This is an inference from the model showing how γ affects metabolic enhancement.

claim: By coupling mitochondrial transport to local glucose levels, whole-cell changes in hexokinase or glucose transporter recruitment can be harnessed to tune the cell's response to spatially heterogeneous glucose concentrations.
source: Thus, by coupling mitochondrial transport to local glucose levels, whole-cell changes in hexokinase or glucose transporter recruitment can be harnessed to tune the cell's response to spatially heterogeneous glucose concentrations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: Glucose-mediated halting of mitochondrial transport is a plausible regulatory mechanism for enhancing metabolism in cases with spatially heterogeneous glucose availability in the neuron.
source: Glucose-mediated halting of mitochondrial transport is shown to be a plausible regulatory mechanism for enhancing metabolism in cases with spatially heterogeneous glucose availability in the neuron.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling work.

claim: Mitochondrial positioning requires both sufficient spatial variation in intracellular glucose and sufficiently low absolute glucose levels compared to the saturation constant of the hexokinase enzyme.
source: Specifically, mitochondrial positioning requires both sufficient spatial variation in intracellular glucose and sufficiently low absolute glucose levels compared to the saturation constant of the hexokinase enzyme.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling work.

claim: For physiologically estimated values, mitochondrial localization to the nodes is expected to occur for glucose levels below approximately 2 mM.
source: For physiologically estimated values, mitochondrial localization to the nodes is expected to occur for glucose levels below approximately 2 mM, comparable to physiological brain glucose concentrations (McNay et al., 2001; John et al., 2008).
evidence: This is calculated from the model using physiological parameter estimates.

claim: Upregulating OGT signaling in cultured cells has been shown to decrease the fraction of motile mitochondria by a factor of three.
source: Upregulating OGT signaling in cultured cells has been shown to decrease the fraction of motile mitochondria by a factor of three, while reducing endogenous OGT nearly doubles the motile fraction, indicating that a substantial number of stationary mitochondria are stopped as a result of OGT activity (Pekkurnaz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published experimental data.

claim: Reducing endogenous OGT nearly doubles the motile fraction of mitochondria.
source: Upregulating OGT signaling in cultured cells has been shown to decrease the fraction of motile mitochondria by a factor of three, while reducing endogenous OGT nearly doubles the motile fraction, indicating that a substantial number of stationary mitochondria are stopped as a result of OGT activity (Pekkurnaz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published experimental data.

claim: A substantial number of stationary mitochondria are stopped as a result of OGT activity.
source: Upregulating OGT signaling in cultured cells has been shown to decrease the fraction of motile mitochondria by a factor of three, while reducing endogenous OGT nearly doubles the motile fraction, indicating that a substantial number of stationary mitochondria are stopped as a result of OGT activity (Pekkurnaz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited experimental observations.

claim: Mitochondria have previously been shown to accumulate at spinal nodes of Ranvier in response to neuronal firing activity.
source: We note that mitochondria have previously been shown to accumulate at spinal nodes of Ranvier in response to neuronal firing activity (Fabricius et al., 1993; Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The glucose-dependent halting mechanism provides an additional driving force for mitochondrial localization near the nodes even in quiescent neurons.
source: The mechanism described here provides an additional driving force for mitochondrial localization near the nodes even in quiescent neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling work.

claim: Both the pentose phosphate pathway and glycolysis generate intermediates that feed back into UDP-GlcNAc production by the hexosamine biosynthetic pathway.
source: In particular, both the pentose phosphate pathway and glycolysis generate intermediates that feed back into UDP-GlcNAc production by the hexosamine biosynthetic pathway (Kruger and von Schaewen, 2003; Shirato et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The activity of the fructose-6-phosphate metabolizing enzyme GFAT is believed to be regulated by intermediates in the hexosamine pathway.
source: For example, the activity of the fructose-6-phosphate metabolizing enzyme GFAT is believed to be regulated by intermediates in the hexosamine pathway (Traxinger and Marshall, 1991) and O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) itself is directly regulated by UDP-GlcNAc levels (Hart et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) itself is directly regulated by UDP-GlcNAc levels.
source: For example, the activity of the fructose-6-phosphate metabolizing enzyme GFAT is believed to be regulated by intermediates in the hexosamine pathway (Traxinger and Marshall, 1991) and O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) itself is directly regulated by UDP-GlcNAc levels (Hart et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The de-GlcNAcylating enzyme OGA exhibits long term regulation of expression in response to altered glucose levels.
source: Other enzymes, such as the de-GlcNAcylating enzyme OGA exhibit long term regulation of expression in response to altered glucose levels (Zou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The predominant form of hexokinase in the brain (HK1) is known to bind reversibly to the mitochondrial membrane, with exchange between a mitochondria-bound and a cytoplasmic state believed to contribute to the regulation of its activity.
source: The predominant form of hexokinase in the brain (HK1) is known to bind reversibly to the mitochondrial membrane, with exchange between a mitochondria-bound and a cytoplasmic state believed to contribute to the regulation of its activity (Golestani et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Release of hexokinase into the cytoplasm would result in more spatially uniform glucose consumption, negating the metabolic enhancement achieved through mitochondrial localization.
source: Release of hexokinase into the cytoplasm would result in more spatially uniform glucose consumption, negating the metabolic enhancement achieved through mitochondrial localization.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the model.

claim: The glucose transporters GLUT3 and GLUT4 have been shown to be recruited to the plasma membrane in response to neuronal firing activity.
source: The glucose transporters GLUT3 (Simpson et al., 2008; Duelli and Kuschinsky, 2001; Weisová et al., 2009) and GLUT4 (Ashrafi et al., 2017) have been shown to be recruited to the plasma membrane in response to neuronal firing activity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Transporter densities are spatially heterogeneous, concentrating near regions of synaptic activity.
source: Interestingly, transporter densities are themselves spatially heterogeneous, concentrating near regions of synaptic activity (Ashrafi et al., 2017; Ashrafi and Ryan, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Hexokinase release from mitochondria into the cytoplasm is known to be triggered at least in part by glucose-6-phosphate, the first byproduct in glucose metabolism.
source: For instance, hexokinase release from mitochondria into the cytoplasm (potentially altering kg) is known to be triggered at least in part by glucose-6-phosphate, the first byproduct in glucose metabolism (Crane and Sols, 1954).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The fraction of glucose funneled into the hexosamine biosynthetic pathway can be modified through feedback inhibition of GFAT by the downstream metabolic product UDP-GlcNAc.
source: The fraction of glucose funneled into the hexosamine biosynthetic pathway (incorporated within ks) can also be modified through feedback inhibition of GFAT by the downstream metabolic product UDP-GlcNAc (Li et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Misregulation of hexokinase has been highlighted as a contributor to several neurological disorders, ranging from depression to schizophrenia.
source: Misregulation of hexokinase has been highlighted as a contributor to several neurological disorders, ranging from depression (Regenold et al., 2012) to schizophrenia (Shan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Neuronal glucose transporter deficiency has been linked to autism spectrum disorders and Alzheimer's disease.
source: Neuronal glucose transporter deficiency has been linked to autism spectrum disorders (Zhao et al., 2010) and Alzheimer's disease (Liu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Defects in mitochondrial transport, with the consequent depletion of mitochondria in distal axonal regions, contribute to peripheral neuropathy disorders.
source: Furthermore, defects in mitochondrial transport, with the consequent depletion of mitochondria in distal axonal regions, contribute to peripheral neuropathy disorders (Baloh, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Glucose-dependent mitochondrial localization provides an additional layer of control, beyond conventionally studied regulatory mechanisms, which allows the cell to respond to spatial heterogeneity in glucose concentration.
source: Glucose-dependent mitochondrial localization provides an additional layer of control, beyond conventionally studied regulatory mechanisms, which allows the cell to respond to spatial heterogeneity in glucose concentration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling work.

claim: The model assumes rapid transport of glucose through glucose transporters, so that the internal concentration of glucose at the nodes where transporters are present is assumed to be fixed.
source: For simplicity, we assume rapid transport of glucose through these transporters, so that the internal concentration of glucose at the nodes where transporters are present is assumed to be fixed.
evidence: This is an explicit assumption made in the model.

claim: The model assumes that all pauses in mitochondrial motility are associated with an O-GlcNAcylation event.
source: Our model employs a highly simplified description of mitochondrial dynamics, which assumes that all pauses are associated with such an O-GlcNAcylation event.
evidence: This is an explicit assumption made in the model.

claim: The model assumes that OGA activity is independent of glucose levels.
source: Although there is evidence indicating long-term glucose deprivation can reduce OGA expression (Zou et al., 2012), for simplicity we assume in our model that OGA activity is independent of glucose levels.
evidence: This is an explicit assumption made in the model.

claim: The model assumes that the rate of UDP-GlcNAc production equals the rate of glucose conversion by hexokinase, scaled by the fraction of G6P that is channeled into the hexosamine biosynthetic pathway.
source: In our model, we assume that the rate of UDP-GlcNAc production equals the rate of glucose conversion by hexokinase, scaled by the fraction of G6P that is channeled into the hexosamine biosynthetic pathway.
evidence: This is an explicit assumption made in the model.

claim: The model makes the extreme case assumption that all intermediates in the conversion from glucose into O-GlcNAcylated Milton are localized to mitochondria, with only the initial glucose substrate capable of diffusing through the cytoplasm.
source: In our model, we make the extreme case assumption that all intermediates are localized to mitochondria, with only the initial glucose substrate capable of diffusing through the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is an explicit assumption made in the model.

claim: Cytoplasmic diffusion of any of the pathway intermediates would attenuate the effect on mitochondrial localization.
source: We note that cytoplasmic diffusion of any of the pathway intermediates would attenuate the effect on mitochondrial localization.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the model assumptions.

claim: The simplified model gives an upper limit on the extent to which mitochondria can localize at high glucose regions through the Milton modification mechanism.
source: Our simplified model thus gives an upper limit on the extent to which mitochondria can localize at high glucose regions through the Milton modification mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the implications of the model assumptions.

claim: The formulation with a continuous mitochondrial density faithfully represents the behavior of simulations with discrete mitochondria.
source: The formulation with a continuous mitochondrial density faithfully represents the behavior of simulations with discrete mitochondria, as illustrated in Figure 2b.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the continuous and discrete models in Figure 2b.

claim: Dimensional analysis indicates that three of the six parameters can be used to define units of time, length, and glucose concentration, leaving three dimensionless groups.
source: Dimensional analysis indicates that three of these parameters can be used to define units of time, length, and glucose concentration, leaving three dimensionless groups.
evidence: This is a result of dimensional analysis of the model.
